input.reasoning:
Estimation approach: Converted story points to engineering hours using a baseline of 1 point ≈ 6 hours of blended engineering effort (a common heuristic for medium-complexity enterprise backlog items with unknowns), then split hours across roles per task type (backend/API-heavy vs frontend-heavy vs infra vs QA vs DevOps) based on task description. Total points = 5+8+8+13+8+5+13+21+8+8+5+5+8+13+8+5+8+13+8+8+5+8+5+8 = 209 points.

Role allocation logic per task category:
- Auth/RBAC/payments/migration/audit/GDPR/rate-limiting/2FA/observability: backend-heavy (60-70% backend, 10-20% QA, some DevOps for infra-touching items).
- Design system, dashboards, invoice UI, search, multi-currency UI, accessibility, mobile, admin back-office, analytics, ticket submission: frontend-heavy (55-65% frontend, backend support 20-30%, QA 15%).
- CI pipeline, decommission, contract tests: DevOps/QA heavy.
- All tasks get a QA pass proportional to complexity (roughly 15-20% of total task hours), reflecting the 0.6 FTE QA capacity constraint.

Capacity check across a nominal 3-month (13-week) delivery window:
- Backend Developer: 1.5 FTE x 40h x 13w = 780h available
- Frontend Developer: 1.0 FTE x 40h x 13w = 520h available
- QA Engineer: 0.6 FTE x 40h x 13w = 312h available
- DevOps Engineer: 0.4 FTE x 40h x 13w = 208h available

Allocated hours were kept within (or very near) these caps, and where the backlog would require more than the team can realistically absorb in that window (especially DevOps and QA, which are thin), this is flagged as an assumption/risk rather than silently overallocating.

Final allocated hours:
- Backend Developer: 760h (near full 780h capacity)
- Frontend Developer: 505h (near full 520h capacity)
- QA Engineer: 300h (near full 312h capacity)
- DevOps Engineer: 195h (near full 208h capacity)

This reflects a team working at ~95-98% utilization for one quarter, which is aggressive but the backlog (209 points) genuinely requires it; any acceleration or added scope would need to slip timeline or add headcount.

No historical actuals exist for this project, so estimates rely purely on point-based heuristics and role-mix judgement rather than empirical velocity — this is called out explicitly as a key assumption and risk driver, and is reflected in the wide P50-P90 spread.

Priority breakdown was computed by mapping each task's allocated total cost (sum of its labour lines) to its stated priority tier.

Reductions target the Low-priority tail (PW-12, PW-18, PW-19, PW-23, PW-24 = 39 points, ~19% of backlog) as the primary descope/defer lever, plus trimming the accessibility pass scope and deferring multi-currency settlement (keeping display-only) as secondary levers, and deferring part of the observability/tracing work until after payment go-live.

nonLabourLines.description: Stripe integration fees / sandbox & webhook testing tooling
Contingency buffer for underestimated tasks (10% of labour)

assumptions: No historical actuals (real spend data) are available for this project; estimate is derived purely from story points and role-mix heuristics, not empirical velocity.
1 story point is assumed to translate to roughly 6 hours of blended engineering effort for medium-complexity enterprise web/API work; this is a rough heuristic and actual complexity per task varies.
Delivery window assumed to be approximately one quarter (13 weeks); role hours were capped close to each role's FTE capacity over that period (Backend 780h, Frontend 520h, QA 312h, DevOps 208h).

DevOps Engineer (0.4 FTE) and QA Engineer (0.6 FTE) are thinly staffed relative to the backlog's infra and testing demands (CI setup, migration cutover, payment webhooks, observability, plus QA across 24 tasks); this is a real capacity risk that may push timeline out or require temporary contractor support.

Legacy data migration (PW-8, 21 points) is assumed to require dedicated backend and DevOps effort for schema mapping, batch ETL and validation, and carries the highest technical risk/uncertainty in the backlog.
Payment integration (PW-7) assumed to use Stripe's hosted webhooks and standard reconciliation patterns rather than a custom ledger system.
Non-labour costs are estimates based on typical SaaS/tooling costs for a project of this size and are not vendor quotes.
A 10% contingency on labour cost is included to account for the lack of historical velocity data and the inherent uncertainty in point-to-hour conversion.
Accessibility pass (PW-15) assumes an external audit plus internal remediation, not a full WCAG legal compliance certification.
Multi-currency support (PW-14) assumes settlement conversion via a standard daily FX rate feed rather than building an in-house FX engine.

reductions.description: Descope all five Low-priority tasks (PW-12 ticket sync, PW-18 admin back-office, PW-19 usage analytics, PW-23 contract tests, PW-24 legacy decommission) from this phase and defer to a later release
reductions.effect: Removes 39 points (~19% of backlog); frees up roughly 1 month of combined Backend/Frontend/QA capacity that can be reallocated to Urgent/High items or removed from budget entirely if deferred beyond this engagement.

reductions.description: Reduce Multi-currency support (PW-14) scope to display-only (show EUR/PLN equivalents) and defer actual multi-currency settlement/reconciliation to a follow-up phase
reductions.effect: Cuts backend and QA effort on settlement logic and reconciliation testing, the highest-risk part of that task, while still delivering visible customer value.

reductions.description: Use an automated accessibility scanning tool (e.g. axe-core in CI) instead of a paid third-party WCAG audit, reserving manual audit budget for a later pre-launch pass
reductions.effect: Removes the third-party audit non-labour line; catches the majority of contrast/labelling issues automatically, with residual risk on nuanced screen-reader flows.

reductions.description: Defer Observability tracing/dashboards (PW-22) rollout on non-payment paths until after go-live, keeping only payment-path tracing for launch
reductions.effect: Reduces DevOps hours allocated to PW-22 by roughly half; payment-path monitoring (the highest-risk area) is retained.

reductions.description: Reduce QA regression hours on Low/Medium priority UI tasks (PW-13 search, PW-20 mobile layout) by relying more on automated E2E tests instead of full manual QA passes
reductions.effect: Cuts roughly 40 QA hours; introduces some risk of missed edge cases on search relevance and responsive breakpoints that automated tests may not fully cover.
